summary:
I've been building out infrastructure for a D&D app I run, TheLongRest, and last week wrapped a feature I'd been circling for a while: Adventure Import. It takes a published adventure I own — text pasted in, not a PDF upload — and has the model derive prep material from it (NPCs, locations, story beats) instead of storing the source text anywhere. That distinction matters for licensing: the source gets purged after 72 hours, and only what a DM explicitly reviews and applies survives. I dogfooded it importing "A Deep and Creeping Darkness" for a one-shot with friends, along with a bug/survey page for them to leave feedback from their phones without needing an account on anything else.

The gnarlier bug of the week was in real-time presence — dice rolls and initiative order broadcasting live between players. Supabase's client reuses one channel per topic under the hood, but I had about ten components each independently creating "their own" channel for the same campaign. Second caller in would throw on channel setup, and closing any one component (like the DM screen) would tear down the shared channel for everyone else on the page until a reload. Fixed it by ref-counting listeners against one shared channel per campaign instead of letting each component own its own.

On the infrastructure side, I finally sat down and looked at four months of power-draw data I'd been logging from my home GPU server and had never actually opened. Built a small dashboard for it — nothing fancy, just server-rendered charts reading a CSV — and the interesting design constraint was making outages visible instead of papered over: gaps in the log are drawn as gaps, not smoothed into a line, because the whole point of collecting the data was to catch the logger going silent, which it had, for two weeks, without anyone noticing.
